title: This, because of that
hookLine: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises (SN 12.21)

cards: You're snappish with someone at dinner. Why? Because you're tired.
Why tired? You slept badly. Why?
You were up late answering messages, because a deadline moved. Why did it move? Because someone else's plan fell through, because of their week, because of theirs.
Pull on any single mood and you find a thread attached to other threads, all the way out. The Buddha put this into a formula so short it would fit on a fortune cookie.

teach.b: The word is paticcasamuppada. Paticca means depending on, leaning on. Samuppada means arising together.
Dependent arising, or dependent origination. In the Connected Discourses, book twelve, the Buddha gives it in four lines.

teach.h: WHEN THIS IS, THAT COMES TO BE.
teach.b: When this is, that comes to be. With the arising of this, that arises.

teach.h: WHEN THIS IS NOT, THAT IS NOT.
teach.b: When this is not, that does not come to be. With the ending of this, that ends. No names, no gods, no story.
Just a pattern. Here's why it matters. The four truths say dukkha has a cause, and that it can end.
Dependent arising explains how both are possible. If dukkha just existed on its own, nothing could be done. But it leans on conditions.
Change the conditions, and it changes. The third and fourth lines are the hopeful ones. There's a well-known moment in the Long Discourses.
Ananda tells the Buddha that dependent arising, though they say it's deep, seems perfectly clear to him. The Buddha stops him.

It is deep, and it looks deep, and because people don't understand it, they get tangled like a ball of string. So two things are true at once: it's simple enough to say over dinner, and deep enough to take a lifetime.
Buddhist schools have unfolded it in different ways, some as a chain across lifetimes, some as the way every moment hangs together. The formula sits underneath them all.

how: Buddhists study dependent arising as a central teaching in every school; Theravada monastics chant its formula, and Mahayana and Tibetan teachers often present it as the key to understanding emptiness.

o: a cycle of luck from life to life
a chain of fate no one can break
dependent arising: this, because of that

games.q: match each part of dependent arising.
p: that does not come to be

s: dependent arising is a story about the gods creating the world
it's a pattern with no names or gods: when this is, that comes to be.
the Buddha told Ananda that dependent arising is deep
Ananda called it clear, and the Buddha said: don't say that; it is deep.
the formula includes how things end, not only how they arise
when this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends.

games.q: you're Ananda. you tell the Buddha that dependent arising, though people call it deep, seems perfectly clear to you. what does he say?
o: don't say that; it is deep, and people get tangled for not understanding it.
then teach it to the others.
games.why: he stops Ananda: it is deep and looks deep, and not understanding it, people get tangled like a ball of string.

practice: Notice the mood you're in right now, flat, restless, content or tense, and name it.
Then ask gently what it's leaning on, maybe sleep, food, a conversation, the weather, and follow one thread back a step or two without judging any of it.
Notice that the mood is changing even as you watch, because its conditions are.

wordCard.voice: Paticcasamuppada. Dependent arising: when this is, that comes to be; when this ends, that ends. Nothing stands on its own.

orig.note: Pali paṭiccasamuppāda, Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda: dependent arising, things arising in dependence on conditions.

carryVoice: Your line: leans on conditions. A feeling that leans on things can also shift with them. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: DN 15 (Mahanidana Sutta), Ananda told not to call it clear
